title: From Zero to Your First Paid AI Project
description: A personal plan that takes you from «I know some AI tools» to money in your account. Built from your answers: what you want to sell, how much time you have, and what is stopping you right now.

modules.title: How AI Freelancing Actually Works
modules.description: See how AI work is really bought and sold — without the hype or the six-figure screenshots. Covers what clients pay for, what they ignore, and the shortest honest path to a first paid task.

lessons.title: Why Your AI Skills Aren't Getting You Paid

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Most people approach this in the same order: learn the tools first, then look for work. It sounds sensible. You would not apply for a driving job without knowing how to drive.

But the people getting paid right now are rarely the ones who know the most tools. They are the ones who can name a job a business already wants done, and say they will do it. The skill is the easy half. The hard half is the sentence you send.

blocks.heading: Clients Don't Buy Tools
blocks.bodyHtml:
A business owner does not wake up wanting AI. They wake up with a newsletter that has not gone out for three weeks.

Compare two replies to the same job post:

«I'm an AI specialist skilled in ChatGPT, Claude and Midjourney.»

«I'll write your weekly newsletter in your voice and hand it over ready to send.»

The first one asks the buyer to imagine what you might do. The second one describes their Tuesday without the problem in it.

blocks.text: Nobody pays for access to a tool they could open themselves.

blocks.heading: The Gap Nobody Warns You About
blocks.bodyHtml:
Here is where most beginners actually stall, and none of it is about skill:

  • No named service — «I can do anything with AI» reads as «I have done nothing yet»
  • No proof — nothing a stranger can look at in ten seconds
  • No price — every conversation stops at «it depends»
  • No routine — five applications in a burst, then nothing for two weeks

Each of these is a sentence you have not written yet. That is genuinely all. Nothing here requires another course.

blocks.question: A business owner posts: «Need help with our weekly newsletter.» Which first reply is strongest?

options.label: I'm an AI specialist with experience in ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini.
I'll write your weekly newsletter in your voice, ready to publish.
I use advanced prompt engineering to produce content very fast.
I've completed several courses on AI writing and content design.

blocks.successBody: The buyer has a job to hand over, not a tool to learn. Naming the finished thing — a newsletter in their voice, ready to send — is what makes a reply feel like relief instead of homework.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about what the person on the other side wants to stop doing themselves this week.

blocks.heading: What a Buyer Checks First
blocks.bodyHtml:
When someone reads your message, they are answering three questions in about eight seconds:

  • Did they understand my problem? Your first line should sound like their job post, not your CV.
  • Have they done this before? One relevant example beats a list of ten unrelated ones.
  • Will this be easy? A clear next step — a price, a timeline, one question — removes the work of deciding.

Notice that none of the three asks which model you used.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Open any freelance platform and read five job posts in a field that interests you.
Copy the exact words buyers use for the outcome they want — not the tools they name.
Write one sentence that offers that outcome, with no tool mentioned at all.
Read it out loud. If it sounds like a description of you rather than of their week, rewrite it.

blocks.heading: The Shortest Honest Path
blocks.bodyHtml:
You do not need to be the best AI operator available. You need to be the person who removes one specific job from someone's week, reliably, for a price they can approve without a meeting.

That is a much smaller target than it first appears. And it is reachable in weeks, not years, because the bar is not talent — it is clarity.

blocks.body: People are not buying AI skills; they are buying a task leaving their list. Skill gets you ready, but a named service, visible proof, a stated price and a weekly routine are what get you paid. Every one of those is a sentence you can write today.

lessons.title: Why Charging for Hours Holds You Back

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Hourly rates feel like the fair way to start. You are new, you do not want to overcharge, and time is something both sides understand.

But there is a trap inside it. AI makes you faster every month — and an hourly rate turns that speed into a pay cut. Finish in one hour what used to take four, and you have just charged yourself a quarter of the fee for the same result.

blocks.heading: The Same Job, Two Ways
blocks.bodyHtml:
A client needs twelve product descriptions. Look at the difference in what you are actually selling:

«£20 per hour, roughly six hours.»

«£180 for twelve product descriptions, delivered Thursday, one round of revisions included.»

The first invites a negotiation about your speed. The second invites a decision about a result. Only one of them gets faster to answer as you get better.

blocks.text: Price the result, and speed becomes your profit instead of your penalty.

blocks.heading: What a Fixed Price Needs
blocks.bodyHtml:
A price is only safe when the shape of the job is decided. Three things do that:

  • A number. Twelve descriptions. Four posts. One landing page. Not «content support».
  • A date. Thursday. Not «soon» — vagueness costs you the weekend.
  • A limit. One round of revisions included, further rounds charged. This single line prevents most unpaid work.

Miss one and the job expands quietly until the fee stops making sense.

blocks.question: You've quoted a fixed price. The client asks for a fifth round of edits. What's the professional move?

options.label: Do them quietly — arguing over edits will only damage the relationship.
Point to the agreed limit and quote a small fee for the extra round.
Explain that AI-assisted work cannot really be revised that many times.
Switch this client to an hourly rate so the extra time gets covered.

blocks.successBody: The limit you agreed is what makes a fixed price work for both sides. Naming it calmly and offering the extra round as a small paid add-on keeps the job profitable without turning it into a conflict.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which answer protects both the relationship and the fee at the same time.

blocks.heading: Packaging Beats Guessing
blocks.bodyHtml:
Once you have priced the same job three times, stop quoting from scratch. Write it down as a package with a name, a scope and a number.

Two effects follow immediately. Buyers decide faster, because there is nothing to work out. And you stop under-pricing on tired days, because the number is no longer a judgement call you make in the moment.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Pick one job you could deliver this week and write it as: quantity, deadline, revision limit.
Put a number on it — the one you would accept without hesitating, not the lowest you would tolerate.
Read the package back and ask whether a stranger could approve it without a call.
If they could not, the scope is still too vague — add the missing number or date.

blocks.heading: When Hourly Still Makes Sense
blocks.bodyHtml:
There is one honest exception: work whose shape genuinely cannot be known in advance. Ongoing support, exploratory research, sitting inside someone else's messy process.

For that, bill by time — but cap it. «Up to eight hours a month, reviewed together before we go over» keeps the openness without handing the client an unlimited claim on your week.

blocks.body: Hourly billing punishes the speed AI gives you. Price the result instead, and make the result safe to price with three details: a quantity, a date and a revision limit. Keep time-based billing only for work whose shape genuinely cannot be known, and cap it.

lessons.title: Your First Paid Task in One Week

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
The advice you usually get is to build a portfolio, then a website, then a brand, and eventually approach clients. It sounds responsible. It is also why most people are still preparing a year later.

There is a shorter route, and it is not a shortcut in the bad sense. It works because a first paid task teaches you more in three days than three months of preparing for one.

blocks.heading: Start From the Task, Not the Career
blocks.bodyHtml:
A first job does not need to fit your long-term plan. It needs to be small, describable and finishable.

«I'm building an AI content agency.»

«I'll turn your ten blog posts into ten LinkedIn posts by Friday for £120.»

The second one can be accepted by a real person today. The first one cannot be accepted at all — there is nothing in it to say yes to.

blocks.text: A career is built out of finished jobs, not out of plans for them.

blocks.heading: The Week, Day by Day
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Days 1–2. Choose one task you can already do well. Write it as quantity, deadline, price.
  • Day 3. Make one sample of it — for a real company you admire, unpaid, unasked. This is your proof.
  • Days 4–6. Send fifteen messages: platform posts, past colleagues, local businesses. Same offer, same sample.
  • Day 7. Follow up with everyone who did not reply. Most first jobs come from the follow-up.

blocks.question: You've sent fifteen messages and received two polite refusals and no other replies. What does that mean?

options.label: The offer is wrong and should be rebuilt from scratch before sending more.
This is a normal week — follow up, then send the next fifteen messages.
The market is saturated and this kind of work is no longer worth selling.
You need a finished website and brand before anyone will take you seriously.

blocks.successBody: Fifteen messages is a small sample, not a verdict. Replies usually arrive after a follow-up, and the second batch tends to be better written than the first — which is exactly how the offer gets sharper.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about how many attempts it takes before you have enough information to judge anything.

blocks.heading: Why the Sample Does the Selling
blocks.bodyHtml:
An unrequested sample answers the only question that matters — can this person actually do the thing — before anyone has to trust you.

It also changes the tone of your message. You are no longer asking for a chance; you are showing something you already made and offering more of it. That difference is felt immediately by the person reading.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Name the task you could deliver this week, in one sentence a stranger would understand.
Pick one real company and make a small sample of that work for them today.
Write the message you'd attach it to — three sentences, no CV, one clear price.
Send it to five people before you allow yourself to edit it again.

blocks.heading: What Counts as Done
blocks.bodyHtml:
The goal of this week is not a good income. It is one transaction: someone paid you, you delivered, both sides were fine with it.

That single event changes what you can say next. You stop describing what you could do and start describing what you have done — and every message after it is easier to write.

blocks.body: The fastest route to a first paid task is a small, describable job, one unrequested sample and fifteen honest messages with a follow-up. Preparation feels safer, but a completed transaction teaches more and changes how you are able to describe yourself.

lessons.title: Why «I Can Do Anything» Wins Nothing

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
When you are starting out, staying open feels like the safe choice. Narrowing down looks like turning away money you cannot afford to turn away.

In practice it works the other way round. A buyer scanning ten profiles is not looking for the most flexible person. They are looking for someone who has clearly done their exact thing before. Breadth reads as inexperience, even when it is genuinely capability.

blocks.heading: Two Profiles, One Buyer
blocks.bodyHtml:
Imagine a shop owner who needs product descriptions rewritten. They open two profiles:

«AI generalist. Writing, design, automation, data, video. Fast and reliable.»

«I rewrite product descriptions for small online shops so they read like a person wrote them.»

The first person might be better at the job. The second one has already answered the only question the buyer had.

blocks.text: Being findable beats being capable, right up until someone hires you.

blocks.heading: What Narrowing Actually Costs
blocks.bodyHtml:
Here is the part that makes it easier to do:

  • You are choosing what to advertise, not what to accept
  • Nothing stops you saying yes to a different job that lands in your inbox
  • You can change the offer next month — nobody is keeping a record
  • You keep every skill you have; you just stop leading with all of them at once

The cost is close to zero. The gain is that strangers can finally tell what you do.

blocks.question: You can write, edit video and build automations. What should your profile headline say?

options.label: Writer, video editor and automation builder available for projects.
I turn long webinars into short clips for coaches who sell online.
Experienced AI generalist helping businesses of all sizes grow.
Flexible freelancer offering content, video and workflow support.

blocks.successBody: A headline that names one job and one kind of buyer lets a stranger recognise themselves in it. Your other skills stay available — they just stop competing for attention in the first line.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which line lets one specific person say «that's my situation» in under three seconds.

blocks.heading: Where a Good Offer Comes From
blocks.bodyHtml:
The strongest first offer usually sits where three things overlap:

  • Something you have already done, even unpaid, even for yourself
  • Something businesses already buy — you can see it in job posts today
  • Something finishable in days, not months

If an idea fails the third test, it is a service for later. Long projects are hard to price, hard to trust and hard to finish while you are still learning how any of this works.

blocks.heading: Try
items: List five things you have made with AI in the last month, paid or not.
Cross out anything that would take longer than a week to deliver.
For each one left, search a freelance platform for that exact job.
Keep the one with the most live listings — demand you can see beats demand you assume.

blocks.heading: Say It in One Sentence
blocks.bodyHtml:
Write your offer as: I help [specific person] with [specific job] so they [specific outcome].

If any bracket still contains the word «businesses» or «content», it is not specific enough yet. «Small online shops» is a person. «Product descriptions» is a job. «Sound like a person wrote them» is an outcome you can be judged on.

blocks.body: Breadth feels safe but reads as inexperience. Pick one job, for one kind of buyer, that you can finish in days and that you can see people buying today. You are choosing what to advertise, not what to accept — and you can change it whenever you like.

lessons.title: How to Size a Service Someone Will Buy

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Once you know what you sell, the next question is how big one unit of it should be. Most beginners get this wrong in the same direction: they make the offer too large, hoping it looks more valuable.

A large offer is harder to price, harder to trust and harder to say yes to. The first purchase is not about value. It is about risk.

blocks.heading: Small Enough to Approve Alone
blocks.bodyHtml:
There is a size below which a person can just decide, and above which they have to ask someone else. Compare:

«Full content strategy and three months of execution.»

«Twelve product descriptions, delivered Thursday, £180.»

The second one gets answered today by the person reading it. The first one goes into a folder called «think about later», which is where offers go to die.

blocks.text: The first sale is not about how much value you offer. It is about how little risk you ask for.

blocks.heading: Three Numbers Make It Safe
blocks.bodyHtml:
A service is properly sized when you can state all three of these without thinking:

  • Quantity. Twelve descriptions. Four posts. One landing page.
  • Delivery date. A weekday, not «soon» and not «within two weeks».
  • Revision limit. One round included, extra rounds priced separately.

Miss any of the three and the job has no edges. Work without edges expands until the fee stops making sense, and the person who absorbs that is always you.

blocks.question: Which of these is sized well enough for a stranger to accept without a call?

options.label: Ongoing content support for your brand, priced monthly by agreement.
Eight LinkedIn posts from your existing blog, sent next Tuesday.
A complete social media audit and strategy tailored to your goals.
Help with your marketing whenever you need an extra pair of hands.

blocks.successBody: A quantity and a date turn an offer into something a person can approve on their own. Everything else on this list needs a conversation first, and most conversations never get scheduled.
blocks.wrongHint: Look for the option where you could count the deliverables and put them in a calendar.

blocks.heading: Two Sizes, Not Ten
blocks.bodyHtml:
Once the small version works, add exactly one larger version — usually the same thing repeated monthly.

Two options is a choice. Five options is a research task, and people postpone research tasks. The small one gets you in the door; the larger one is what you offer once they already trust you, which is a much easier conversation.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Write your offer with a quantity, a delivery day and a revision limit.
Read it as if you were the buyer: could you say yes without asking anyone?
If not, cut the scope in half and read it again.
Write the monthly version of the same thing in one line underneath.

blocks.heading: When the Job Is Genuinely Big
blocks.bodyHtml:
Some real work does not fit in a week. The answer is not to shrink it dishonestly — it is to sell the first stage on its own.

A paid audit, a sample batch, a single page before the whole site. The client gets a small decision and real output; you get paid while both sides find out whether you work well together.

blocks.body: Size the offer so one person can approve it alone: a quantity, a delivery day and a revision limit. Keep two options rather than five, and split genuinely large work into a paid first stage instead of asking for a big commitment from a stranger.

lessons.title: Test the Offer Before You Build It

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
The tempting next step is to prepare: a portfolio site, a price sheet, a set of templates. It feels like progress because it is visible work you fully control.

But none of it answers the only question that matters yet — does anyone want this? That answer costs about an hour to get, and it changes what you would have spent the week building.

blocks.heading: Demand You Can See
blocks.bodyHtml:
You do not need a survey. You need evidence that money is already moving:

  • Live job posts asking for this exact task, posted in the last month
  • Other freelancers selling it — competition is proof, not a warning
  • Businesses visibly doing it badly themselves

If you find none of the three after twenty minutes of looking, the problem is the offer, not your search skills.

blocks.text: Competition is the cheapest proof that someone is willing to pay.

blocks.heading: The One-Hour Test
blocks.bodyHtml:
Take the sentence you wrote and put it in front of five real people who could plausibly buy. Not friends, and not a public post — five direct messages.

You are not selling yet. You are asking one question: «Is this something you deal with?» The replies tell you more than any amount of preparation, because they arrive in the buyer's own words, which you can then reuse.

blocks.question: Four people reply that they already handle this in-house and it works fine. What now?

options.label: Lower your price until handling it in-house stops being worth it.
Ask what the annoying part of handling it in-house actually is.
Move on to a completely different field where nobody says this.
Send the same message again to a much larger group of people.

blocks.successBody: «We handle it ourselves» is rarely the end of the conversation. The annoying part of doing it in-house is usually the real offer, and it is described to you in the buyer's own words if you ask.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which reply gives you new information rather than repeating what you already tried.

blocks.heading: What a Good Signal Looks Like
blocks.bodyHtml:
You are not waiting for enthusiasm. You are watching for three quieter things:

  • They describe the problem back to you in more detail than you used
  • They ask how much or how long — a question about logistics, not about interest
  • They mention who currently does it and why that is unsatisfying

Any one of those means keep going. Polite agreement with no detail means the problem is not painful enough to pay for.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Find five businesses that fit your buyer description exactly.
Send each a short message asking whether this task is something they deal with.
Record the replies word for word — that phrasing becomes your offer text.
If nobody responds after a follow-up, change one thing: the buyer or the task.

blocks.heading: Then Build, But Only What Is Needed
blocks.bodyHtml:
Once someone has shown interest, build exactly what the next conversation requires and nothing else. Usually that is one sample and a price.

The site, the brand and the templates can come later, paid for by work you have already done. Almost every freelancer who stalls for months stalled while building things nobody had asked to see.

blocks.body: Before building anything, look for demand you can see and send five direct messages. Watch for detail, logistics questions and complaints about the current solution rather than enthusiasm. Then build only what the next conversation needs — usually one sample and a price.

modules.title: A Profile That Wins Work
modules.description: Build a profile and portfolio that work with zero client history. Covers proof you can create yourself, the first three lines that decide everything, and samples that read as real work.

lessons.title: The First Three Lines Decide Everything

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Most profile advice is about completeness: fill every field, list every skill, upload a good photo. So people write a full page and wonder why nothing happens.

Almost nobody reads a full page. A buyer with fifteen applications open gives each one a few seconds, and that decision is made in the first three lines — the headline and the opening sentence.

blocks.heading: Write for Recognition, Not Admiration
blocks.bodyHtml:
The opening is not where you impress. It is where the reader recognises themselves.

«Detail-oriented professional passionate about leveraging AI to deliver results.»

«If your blog posts never make it to social media, that is the part I take over.»

The first sentence describes you and could belong to anyone. The second describes their week and could only belong to someone who has seen the problem.

blocks.text: A buyer is not deciding whether you are good. They are deciding whether you understood.

blocks.heading: Words That Cost You Attention
blocks.bodyHtml:
Some phrases are so common they now read as noise:

  • «Passionate about…» — every profile says it, so it carries no information
  • «Results-driven» — a claim with nothing behind it
  • «I'm new but eager to learn» — honest, but it asks the buyer to take the risk
  • «Any project, big or small» — reads as «nothing in particular»

Cutting all four usually shortens a profile by a third and makes it noticeably sharper.

blocks.question: Which opening line is most likely to get a reply from a busy buyer?

options.label: Passionate AI enthusiast with strong attention to detail and deadlines.
Your product photos are fine — the descriptions under them are losing sales.
Experienced freelancer offering high quality work at competitive rates.
I am new to this platform but very motivated to prove myself to clients.

blocks.successBody: The line that names something specific about the buyer's situation proves you looked. Everything else on this list describes the writer, and the reader has no reason to care about the writer yet.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which line could only have been written by someone who looked at this particular business.

blocks.heading: The Shape That Works
blocks.bodyHtml:
Three short paragraphs are enough:

  • The problem, in their words, in one sentence
  • What you deliver, with a quantity and a timeframe
  • One piece of proof — a link, a sample, a specific result

Then stop. Everything after this point is read only by people who have already decided to consider you, and they are looking for a reason to say yes, not more description.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Open your current profile and read only the first three lines out loud.
Count how many words describe you rather than the buyer's problem.
Rewrite the opening so the first sentence is about them, not you.
Delete every phrase from the list above, then read it again.

blocks.heading: One Profile per Offer
blocks.bodyHtml:
If you genuinely sell two different things, write two versions and send whichever one fits.

Trying to cover both in one profile produces the vague opening we started with. A tailored page takes ten minutes to adapt and is the single clearest signal that you read the job post before applying.

blocks.body: Your profile is judged in three lines. Open with the buyer's problem in their own words, follow with what you deliver and by when, then give one piece of proof and stop. Cut every phrase that could appear on anyone else's profile.
blocks.nextTeaser: Next: the proof you can create today, without a single past client.

lessons.title: Proof You Can Make Today

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
The obvious problem with a first job is that you need experience to get it, and a job to get experience. It looks like a genuine deadlock, and it stops a lot of people for months.

It is not one. Buyers do not actually require past clients — they require evidence that the work will be good. Those are different things, and only one of them needs someone else's permission.

blocks.heading: What Counts as Evidence
blocks.bodyHtml:
A buyer looking at a sample is asking one question: does this person produce work at the standard I need?

«I don't have client work yet, but I'm confident I can do this.»

«Here are three descriptions I rewrote for a shop like yours — same products, different result.»

Nobody asks whether the second one was paid. The output answers the question by existing.

blocks.text: Nobody asks whether the sample was paid for. They only ask whether it is good.

blocks.heading: Four Kinds of Proof You Control
blocks.bodyHtml:
• The unrequested rework. Take a real company's page and redo it. Show both versions.
  • The self-project. Something you built for yourself, with the numbers if you have them.
  • The teardown. A short breakdown of what is wrong with something and how you would fix it.
  • The process note. How you actually work, in six lines — this reassures nervous buyers.

Each takes an afternoon. None requires anyone's permission.

blocks.question: You have no clients yet. Which sample is most persuasive to a shop owner?

options.label: A certificate from a well-reviewed online course about AI writing.
Their own product page, rewritten, shown next to the original text.
A long document explaining your writing process and general approach.
A list of the AI tools you use, with your experience level in each.

blocks.successBody: Work done on their own page removes every act of imagination the buyer would otherwise have to perform. It also proves you spent real effort before being paid, which most applicants never do.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which option requires the buyer to imagine the least before deciding.

blocks.heading: Show the Before
blocks.bodyHtml:
A sample on its own is decoration. A sample next to what it replaced is an argument.

Put the original and your version side by side, and add one line explaining what changed and why. That line is what turns «nice writing» into «this person knows what they are doing» — and it is the part almost everyone leaves out.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Pick one real business you would genuinely like to work with.
Redo one small piece of their work — a page, a post, a workflow.
Put the before and after side by side with one line explaining the change.
Save it somewhere you can link to in under five seconds.

blocks.heading: Three Is Enough
blocks.bodyHtml:
You do not need a portfolio of twenty pieces. Three strong samples in the same category beat twenty mixed ones, because they show a standard rather than a range.

Mixed portfolios quietly repeat the mistake from the last unit: they say «I can do anything», and the buyer reads «nothing in particular».

blocks.body: You do not need past clients, you need evidence. Rework a real company's page, build something for yourself, or take one thing apart and show how you would fix it — then present it beside what it replaced with a line about what changed. Three focused samples are enough.
blocks.nextTeaser: Next: how to present those samples so they read as real work rather than practice.

lessons.title: Samples That Read Like Real Work

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Two people can produce identical work and get completely different responses to it. The difference is almost never quality — it is packaging.

A sample presented as an exercise gets read as an exercise. The same file presented as a delivery gets read as evidence that you have done this before, because that is what a delivery looks like.

blocks.heading: Label It as Work, Not Practice
blocks.bodyHtml:
The framing sentence above a sample does most of the work.

«A practice piece I made while learning, feedback welcome.»

«Rewrite of a live product page — original on the left, new version on the right.»

Both are honest. Only one of them asks the reader to lower their expectations before they have looked at anything.

blocks.text: Apologising for a sample teaches the reader to judge it gently — and to hire someone else.

blocks.heading: What a Buyer Checks in a Sample
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Is it in my world? Same industry, or close enough to imagine.
  • Is it finished? No placeholder text, no half-formatted lists, no broken links.
  • Can I see the decision? One line on why it changed beats three paragraphs of process.
  • How fast can I look? Anything requiring a download loses most readers.

Three of those four are presentation, not skill — which is good news, because presentation is quick to fix.

blocks.question: Where should a sample live so that the most buyers actually look at it?

options.label: A shared document link that opens instantly in the browser window.
A zip archive attached to the message, ready for them to download.
A portfolio site that asks for an email address before showing work.
A design file that opens properly in professional editing software.

blocks.successBody: Every extra step between the message and the work removes a share of readers. A link that opens instantly in the browser is read by nearly everyone; anything requiring a download or a sign-up is read by few.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about how many actions the buyer has to take before they see anything at all.

blocks.heading: Match the Sample to the Job
blocks.bodyHtml:
Sending three samples signals «pick one that fits». Sending the single closest one signals «I read your post».

If nothing you have matches, make the match: spend an hour producing a small piece in their exact category before you reply. That hour is the cheapest advantage available to a beginner, and almost nobody spends it.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Open each of your samples the way a stranger would, from the link you send.
Time how long it takes before real work appears on screen.
Remove any wording that frames the piece as practice or as a test.
Add one line above each explaining what changed and why it matters.

blocks.heading: Keep It Current
blocks.bodyHtml:
Once real jobs arrive, replace samples with paid work as soon as a client agrees. Ask at delivery, while they are pleased — «may I show this as an example?» is almost always answered yes in that moment.

Waiting a month to ask turns an easy yes into an awkward request about something they have stopped thinking about.

blocks.body: Package samples as deliveries, not practice: one link that opens instantly, work from the buyer's world, and a single line explaining the decision behind it. Send the closest match rather than a set, and swap in paid work by asking at delivery, while the client is pleased.

modules.title: How Freelance Work Flows
modules.description: Understand the shape of a freelance job from first message to final payment — without prior experience. Covers briefs, deadlines, revisions, and what «professional» actually looks like.

lessons.title: What a Freelance Job Actually Looks Like

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
People imagine freelancing as a series of creative tasks with money attached. That is roughly ten per cent of it, and it is the part nobody struggles with.

The rest is a small, repeatable sequence: enquiry, agreement, work, delivery, payment. Knowing the shape of it removes most of the anxiety, because you stop being surprised by steps that were always going to happen.

blocks.heading: The Five Stages
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Enquiry — someone asks whether you can help; you find out what they actually need
  • Agreement — scope, price, date and revision limit, written down
  • Work — with one visible check-in if it runs longer than a few days
  • Delivery — the files, plus a short note on what to look at
  • Payment — invoiced immediately, chased politely if late

Every job is this. The differences are in size, not structure.

blocks.text: Most freelance stress comes from skipping stage two and discovering it later.

blocks.heading: Where Beginners Lose Money
blocks.bodyHtml:
Almost every painful first job traces back to the same shortcut:

«Sounds good, I'll get started and we can figure out the details as we go.»

«Twelve descriptions, delivered Thursday, £180, one round of revisions. Shall I start?»

The second sentence takes twenty seconds to write and prevents the argument that otherwise arrives in week three.

blocks.question: A client asks you to start today and says you can «sort out the details later». What do you do?

options.label: Start straight away — showing enthusiasm early builds a better relationship.
Send one short message with scope, price and date, then begin work.
Ask them to sign a formal contract drafted before any work happens.
Decline politely, since clients who rush at the start are unreliable.

blocks.successBody: A three-line message covers you without slowing anything down. A full contract is often too heavy for a small first job, and starting with nothing written is how scope quietly doubles.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which option protects the work without adding a delay the client will resent.

blocks.heading: Speed Beats Polish at the Start
blocks.bodyHtml:
At the enquiry stage, the freelancer who replies within an hour wins a surprising share of jobs — often against people with better portfolios.

A buyer with a problem is looking for it to stop being their problem. Being reachable is the first evidence that it will, and it is the one advantage that costs you nothing to have.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Write the three-line agreement message you will reuse for every job.
Leave blanks for quantity, price, date and revision limit only.
Save it where you can paste it from your phone in under ten seconds.
Use it on the very next enquiry, even a small or informal one.

blocks.heading: One Check-In, Not Silence
blocks.bodyHtml:
For anything longer than three days, send one short update halfway through — a sentence and a fragment of the work.

It costs two minutes and removes the client's quiet worry that nothing is happening. That worry is what turns into anxious messages, unnecessary calls and, eventually, a client who does not come back.

blocks.body: Every job follows the same five stages, and almost every bad experience comes from skipping the agreement. Reply fast, write three lines covering quantity, price, date and revisions, send one check-in on longer work, and invoice the moment you deliver.
blocks.nextTeaser: Next: how to run the conversation that turns a vague request into a clear brief.

lessons.title: The Brief Is Your Safety Net

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Clients rarely know how to brief. They describe the outcome they picture and assume the rest is obvious, because to them it is.

Filling in the gaps yourself feels helpful and confident. It is also where most disputes begin — you deliver exactly what you understood, and they receive something that was never in their head.

blocks.heading: Four Questions That Prevent Most Problems
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Who is this for? Their customer, described as a person
  • What should it make happen? A sale, a reply, a booking
  • What have you tried? Tells you what they already dislike
  • What would make this a no? The fastest way to hear their real constraints

Four questions, two minutes, and the answers usually contain the exact phrases you will use in the work.

blocks.text: Every assumption you do not check is one you have quietly agreed to pay for.

blocks.heading: Ask Before You Guess
blocks.bodyHtml:
Beginners avoid questions because asking feels like admitting you do not know. It reads as the opposite.

«Got it, I'll put something together and you can tell me what you think.»

«Before I start — is this aimed at first-time buyers or people who already know you?»

The second one is what an experienced person sounds like. It also saves the rewrite that the first one guarantees.

blocks.question: A client's brief is one line: «make it more engaging». What is the best response?

options.label: Deliver a livelier version and let their reaction reveal what they meant.
Ask which recent piece of theirs felt engaging and what made it work.
Explain that engagement depends on many factors outside your control.
Add humour and questions, since that is what usually reads as engaging.

blocks.successBody: Vague words mean something specific to the person saying them. Asking for an example they already liked converts an adjective into a target you can actually hit, in their own words.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which option turns a subjective word into something concrete you can check against.

blocks.heading: Write It Back to Them
blocks.bodyHtml:
After the questions, send a short summary: what you will produce, for whom, by when, and what success looks like.

Ask them to confirm. That message is the entire contract for a small job — and if their reply corrects something, you have just avoided a rewrite while it still costs nothing.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Save the four questions somewhere you can paste them into a message.
Add one question specific to what you sell, in the client's language.
Practise on a real job post: write the questions you would send today.
Draft the summary message you would send once they answered.

blocks.heading: When They Cannot Answer
blocks.bodyHtml:
Sometimes a client genuinely does not know who their customer is or what success looks like. That is not a bad client — it is a bigger job wearing a small one's clothes.

Say so plainly and offer a short paid first stage to work it out together. Doing that unpaid, inside a fixed fee, is the most common way a profitable job turns into an unprofitable one.

blocks.body: Clients brief in outcomes and leave the specifics to you. Ask who it is for, what it should make happen, what they have tried and what would make it a no — then write the answers back and ask them to confirm. If they cannot answer, that is a paid first stage, not free thinking.
blocks.nextTeaser: Next: delivering in a way that makes rehiring you the obvious choice.

lessons.title: Delivering Like Someone They Will Rehire

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Delivery looks like the end of the job. In practice it is the audition for the next one, and it is decided by things that have nothing to do with the quality of the work.

Two freelancers can send identical files. One gets «thanks» and silence; the other gets rehired next month. The difference is usually thirty seconds of framing.

blocks.heading: Never Send Files Alone
blocks.bodyHtml:
A bare attachment makes the client do the work of understanding what they received.

«Here you go, let me know if you need changes.»

«Twelve descriptions attached. I kept the delivery promise in every one — that was the part missing from the originals. Anything you'd like adjusted, send it by Friday and it's included.»

The second version tells them what to look at, why you did it, and when the door closes.

blocks.text: Delivery is not the end of the job. It is the audition for the next one.

blocks.heading: Four Lines Worth Sending
blocks.bodyHtml:
• What is attached, in plain counts
  • One decision you made and the reason for it
  • What you would do next, if they wanted more
  • The revision window, stated as a date

The third line is the one almost nobody writes, and it is the one that turns a single job into repeat work without ever sounding like a pitch.

blocks.question: You deliver on time and the client replies «thanks». What is the strongest follow-up?

options.label: Say thank you as well and wait for them to come back with more work.
Ask whether you can show the piece as an example, and name what is next.
Send a list of every other service you offer with your full price list.
Offer a discount on their next order so they have a reason to return.

blocks.successBody: Asking at delivery, while they are pleased, is when permission is easiest to get — and naming one obvious next step costs nothing. A full price list asks them to make a decision they were not preparing to make.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which option uses the moment when the client is most satisfied with you.

blocks.heading: Invoice Immediately
blocks.bodyHtml:
Send the invoice with the delivery, not a few days later. Waiting feels polite but it detaches the payment from the moment the client is most pleased with the work.

Put a due date on it — «payable within 7 days» — because an invoice with no date is treated as no particular hurry, and that is how a two-week wait becomes a two-month one.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Write your standard delivery message with the four lines above.
Leave blanks only for the counts, the decision and the revision date.
Add one line asking permission to use the work as a sample.
Attach your invoice template to the same message so both go together.

blocks.heading: When They Ask for More Than Agreed
blocks.bodyHtml:
Extra requests after delivery are normal and not a sign of a difficult client. They are just testing where the edge is.

Point at the agreed limit without apology and price the extra: «that's outside the round we agreed — happy to do it for £40, or I can include it in the next batch». Calm and specific keeps the relationship and the fee at the same time.

blocks.body: Never send files alone. Say what is attached, one decision you made, what you would do next and when revisions close — then invoice immediately with a due date. Ask permission to use the work as a sample while the client is still pleased, and price extras calmly instead of absorbing them.

modules.title: Where the Work Actually Is
modules.description: Find the platforms and channels where AI work is bought today. Covers Upwork, Fiverr, Contra and LinkedIn side by side, and which one fits the offer you picked.

lessons.title: The Four Places AI Work Gets Bought

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
«Find clients» is advice that sounds actionable and is not. Clients are not in one place, and the four places they are in behave completely differently.

Picking the wrong one wastes months. Not because you are bad at selling, but because you are standing in a room where nobody is buying what you brought.

blocks.heading: Bidding Marketplaces
blocks.bodyHtml:
Upwork and similar sites work like a job board where you apply. Buyers post a task, dozens reply, one gets picked.

What this rewards: fast, specific replies to fresh posts and a narrow profile. What it punishes: generic applications and waiting a day to answer. Expect to send many messages for each job at the start — that ratio improves once you have reviews.

blocks.heading: Product Marketplaces
blocks.bodyHtml:
Fiverr and its equivalents work the other way round. You publish a fixed offer and buyers come to you.

This suits a service you can define exactly — «twelve product descriptions, three days». It rewards a sharp title and a clear sample, and it punishes anything that needs a conversation before the price makes sense.

blocks.text: On one platform you chase the work. On another the work has to find you. Both are jobs.

blocks.question: You sell a fixed, well-defined service and hate writing applications. Where should you start?

options.label: A bidding marketplace, because that is where the most work is posted.
A product marketplace, where a fixed offer is listed and buyers come.
A professional network, posting about your work to build an audience.
Direct outreach, contacting local businesses one at a time by email.

blocks.successBody: A fixed, repeatable service is exactly what a product marketplace is built to sell. The other three channels all need you to write something new for every opportunity, which is the part you would avoid.
blocks.wrongHint: Match the channel to the shape of your offer and to the work you will actually keep doing.

blocks.heading: Professional Networks
blocks.bodyHtml:
LinkedIn and similar places are slower and pay better. Nobody is browsing for a freelancer; they notice you over weeks and contact you when something breaks.

This rewards showing work in public and being visibly specific. It punishes impatience — the first month usually produces nothing, and most people quit inside that window.

blocks.heading: Direct Outreach
blocks.bodyHtml:
The fourth channel is contacting businesses yourself. It has no competition, no fees and no algorithm, and it is the only one that works on day one.

It also has the lowest reply rate, so it only pays when the message is specific enough to be obviously about them. That is the subject of the next unit.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Write down which of the four channels matches the offer you defined earlier.
Spend twenty minutes on it looking for live demand for your exact service.
Note how many relevant listings or targets you found in that time.
If you found fewer than five, try a second channel before writing anything.

blocks.body: There are four channels and they reward different things: bidding sites reward speed and narrowness, product marketplaces reward a fixed offer, professional networks reward patience and visibility, direct outreach rewards specificity. Match the channel to your offer instead of trying all four badly.
blocks.nextTeaser: Next: what these platforms actually do to someone with no reviews yet.

lessons.title: How Platforms Treat a Newcomer

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Every platform tells newcomers the same thing: complete your profile and start applying. Then nothing happens, and people conclude the market is saturated.

The market is fine. What is happening is that these systems are built to reduce risk for buyers, and a new account is unproven risk. Knowing exactly how that works changes what you do in the first month.

blocks.heading: The First-Review Problem
blocks.bodyHtml:
Ranking is driven by completed jobs and ratings. With none of either, you are shown last — so the first job is much harder than the tenth, and it is not a fair test of your ability.

The practical response is to treat job one as a cost of entry: smaller, quicker, priced to be an easy yes. Not free, and not underpriced forever — just small enough that a stranger risks it.

blocks.text: The first job is not a fair test of your work. It is a test of how little risk you ask for.

blocks.heading: What Actually Moves the Needle
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Speed. Replying within the first hour beats a better application sent tomorrow.
  • Fit. Ten targeted applications outperform fifty copied ones, and cost less time.
  • Completion. Two finished small jobs unlock more than one large unfinished one.
  • Communication scores. Answering quickly is measured on most platforms.

None of these require experience. All of them are available on your first day.

blocks.question: You have no reviews. A small £60 job and a £900 project are both open. Which do you pursue?

options.label: The larger project, because one good job is worth more than several small.
The smaller job, because a completed review makes the next one reachable.
Both at once, so that whichever answers first becomes your starting point.
Neither yet — build a stronger profile first, then apply to larger work.

blocks.successBody: With no history, a buyer offering £900 has many safer options than you. A completed small job produces the review that makes the larger ones realistic, usually within a few weeks rather than months.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which choice changes your position on the platform rather than just your bank balance.

blocks.heading: Fees Are Not the Enemy
blocks.bodyHtml:
Platform fees look painful — a fifth of your first jobs can disappear. Beginners often try to move clients off-platform to avoid them, which risks the account that produced the client.

Think of the fee as paid distribution. You are buying access to buyers who already trust the payment system, which is the thing you cannot provide yourself yet.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Find the smallest job on your chosen platform that matches your offer exactly.
Write an application that names something specific from their post in line one.
Send it within the hour, and note the time you sent it.
Repeat daily for a week and count replies rather than jobs won.

blocks.heading: What Changes After Three Reviews
blocks.bodyHtml:
The shift is sharper than people expect. Around the third completed job, buyers start contacting you instead of the other way round, and your ranking stops burying you.

That is the real goal of month one — not income. Three small completed jobs are worth more than one lucky large one, because they change the system's opinion of you.

blocks.body: Platforms rank by completed work, so a new account is shown last. Answer fast, apply narrowly, and take the smallest job that fits until you have around three reviews — that is when buyers begin approaching you. Treat fees as paid distribution rather than a loss.
blocks.nextTeaser: Next: choosing one channel and working it properly instead of spreading yourself thin.

lessons.title: Pick One Channel and Work It

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Faced with four channels, the instinct is to try all of them. It feels thorough and it is the most common way people spend three months producing nothing.

Each channel has a warm-up cost — profile, samples, learning what gets answered. Split across four, none of them ever gets past the cold start, and each looks like it failed.

blocks.heading: One Channel, Four Weeks
blocks.bodyHtml:
Give a single channel four weeks of consistent effort before judging it.

«I tried Upwork, Fiverr and LinkedIn, none of them worked.»

«I sent fifteen targeted applications a week on one site for a month, tracked replies, and changed the opening line twice.»

Only the second one produced information you can act on.

blocks.text: Four channels tried for a week each teaches you nothing at all.

blocks.heading: Measure Replies, Not Jobs
blocks.bodyHtml:
Jobs won is a bad early metric — the numbers are too small to learn from. Reply rate is the one that tells you what to fix:

  • No replies at all — the opening line or the channel is wrong
  • Replies but no jobs — price, samples or the follow-up is wrong
  • Jobs but no repeat work — delivery is fine, the ending is weak

Each symptom points at one thing to change, which is a much smaller problem than «it is not working».

blocks.question: Three weeks in: people reply, ask questions, then go quiet after your price. What should you change?

options.label: The channel, since these buyers are clearly not able to pay properly.
How the price is presented — its scope, its packaging and what is included.
The opening line of your message, so that more people reply to you.
Your samples, because the work is evidently not impressing them enough.

blocks.successBody: Replies prove the opening works and the samples were good enough to start a conversation. Losing people at the price means the number arrived without enough shape around it — scope, deliverables and a date.
blocks.wrongHint: Look at which stage the conversation actually stops, and change only that stage.

blocks.heading: A Number You Can Hit
blocks.bodyHtml:
Set a weekly action target rather than an outcome target. Fifteen targeted applications, or twenty direct messages, or three public posts plus ten comments.

Outcomes are not under your control and produce guilt. Actions are, and hitting the number for four weeks is what generates the data you need to make the next decision.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Choose one channel and write the weekly number you will hit.
Put it in your calendar as a repeating block, not a to-do item.
Track two columns only: messages sent and replies received.
Review after four weeks and change exactly one thing based on the pattern.

blocks.heading: When to Actually Switch
blocks.bodyHtml:
Switch channels when you have hit your weekly number for four weeks and the reply rate stayed near zero after two changes to the opening.

That is a real signal. Quitting in week two because it felt discouraging is not — and telling those two situations apart is most of what separates people who get there from people who conclude the market is full.

blocks.body: Trying four channels at once means none of them warms up. Pick one, set a weekly action number you control, and track replies rather than jobs — the stage where conversations stop tells you the single thing to fix. Switch only after four consistent weeks and two real changes.

modules.title: Getting Real Output From AI
modules.description: Stop getting generic answers and start getting usable drafts. Covers context, constraints, iteration, and the difference between asking and briefing.

lessons.title: Why Your First Prompt Disappoints

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Most people try an AI tool, get a flat and generic answer, and quietly decide it is overrated. It feels like a fair conclusion — you asked a clear question and got something that reads like a brochure.

But the problem is almost never the model. The first prompt is a guess, and the answer you got is an accurate response to that guess. Vague input does not produce a vague answer. It produces a confident wrong one.

blocks.heading: You Are Briefing, Not Asking
blocks.bodyHtml:
Think about handing a task to a freelancer. You would not write «make me a logo» and walk away.

«Write a post about productivity.»

«Write a short post for freelancers who lose focus after lunch. One practical idea, no motivational language, under 120 words.»

The second is not longer for the sake of it. Every extra phrase removes a decision the tool would otherwise have made badly.

blocks.text: The words you leave out are the words it has to invent.

blocks.heading: Three Things Every Prompt Needs
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Who it is for — «shop owners selling handmade jewellery», not «customers»
  • What it should achieve — «one idea they can use today», not «be engaging»
  • What to avoid — «no exclamation marks, under 120 words»

Miss one and the answer drifts. Include all three and the first draft is usually close enough to edit rather than rewrite.

blocks.question: Your first answer comes back generic and bland. What is the most useful next step?

options.label: Try a different AI tool, since this one clearly handles writing poorly.
Name what is wrong with the answer and add it as an instruction.
Find a long prompt template online and paste it in place of yours.
Send the same request again and hope the second attempt is better.

blocks.successBody: A weak first answer is a list of missing instructions. Naming what is wrong — too formal, too long, wrong example — and adding it is faster than switching tools or hunting for templates.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which option uses the information the bad answer just gave you.

blocks.heading: Why This Matters for Paid Work
blocks.bodyHtml:
A client is not paying for access to a tool. They are paying because you get usable output on the first or second attempt while they would spend an afternoon on it.

That gap is your entire margin. It comes from knowing what to specify, not from knowing a secret phrase — and it is the reason a clear brief is a professional skill rather than a trick.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Take a prompt you used recently and check it for the three elements above.
Add whatever is missing and run it again without changing anything else.
Compare the two answers side by side and note which phrase caused the change.
Save the improved version — it is the first entry in your own prompt library.

blocks.heading: A Test Before You Send
blocks.bodyHtml:
Read your prompt and ask: could a competent stranger do this task with only these words?

If the answer is no, the model cannot either. This one question catches most weak prompts before you waste a round on them, and it costs about five seconds.

blocks.body: A disappointing answer is usually a well-executed vague request. Say who it is for, what it should achieve and what to avoid, then treat the first result as a draft you correct rather than a verdict on the tool. Your value to a client is the speed of that loop.
blocks.nextTeaser: Next: giving the model a role and real constraints, so the output stops sounding like everyone else's.

lessons.title: Give It a Role and Real Constraints

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Once your prompts contain the basics, the next complaint is different: the answers are correct but forgettable. Everything sounds like it came from the same polite, careful stranger.

That happens because you asked for a task without saying who is performing it. Given no role, the model picks the safest average one — and average is exactly what nobody pays for.

blocks.heading: A Role Is Not a Costume
blocks.bodyHtml:
«Act as a world-class expert» does almost nothing, because it describes status rather than behaviour.

«You are an expert copywriter with 20 years of experience.»

«Write like someone who has run this shop for ten years: plain words, no adjectives, mentions the delivery time in every description.»

The second one is instructions disguised as a role. That is what actually changes the output.

blocks.text: A role only helps when it tells the model what to do differently.

blocks.heading: Constraints That Do Real Work
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Length — «under 60 words» beats «keep it short»
  • Banned words — «never use: unlock, elevate, seamless, journey»
  • Structure — «one sentence of problem, three bullets, one closing line»
  • Reference — «match the tone of the example below»

The last one is the strongest. One real example teaches more about voice than a paragraph of adjectives ever will.

blocks.question: A client says the drafts «don't sound like us». What fixes this fastest?

options.label: Ask the model to write in a warmer, friendlier and more human tone.
Paste two pieces they wrote and ask it to match that exact voice.
Tell it to act as a senior brand strategist with deep experience.
Rewrite each sentence yourself until the text finally feels right.

blocks.successBody: Voice is easier to show than to describe. Two real examples give the model something concrete to match, while adjectives like warmer or more human mean different things to every reader.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which option gives the model information it does not already have.

blocks.heading: Build the Brief Once
blocks.bodyHtml:
For a repeat client, write the role and constraints once and reuse them at the top of every request: their voice rules, their banned words, their format, one strong example.

This is the quiet reason experienced freelancers are faster. Not better prompts in the moment — a standing brief they stopped rewriting weeks ago.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Pick a company you would like to work with and find two things they published.
Write a six-line brief: who is speaking, length, structure, banned words.
Run the same task with and without that brief attached.
Keep the brief in a file — it becomes a deliverable clients will pay for on its own.

blocks.heading: Know When to Stop Steering
blocks.bodyHtml:
Constraints have a limit. Past a point, adding rules makes output stiff and repetitive, because you have removed every choice the model had.

If a draft has become mechanical, cut the newest three rules rather than adding a fourth. The goal is a narrow lane, not a locked cage.

blocks.body: Vague roles change nothing; roles that describe behaviour change everything. Add length, banned words, structure and — most powerfully — a real example to match. Write the brief once per client and reuse it, and remove rules when the output turns stiff.
blocks.nextTeaser: Next: why the second prompt, not the first, is where the usable work appears.

lessons.title: The Second Prompt Is the Real One

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
There is a belief that skilled users write one perfect prompt and receive finished work. It is comforting, because it suggests the skill is a phrase you could look up.

What actually happens is closer to editing. The first answer is information about your instructions; the second is where the work appears. People who expect this get results faster than people hunting for the perfect opening line.

blocks.heading: Read the Draft as a Diagnosis
blocks.bodyHtml:
Every flaw in the output points at a missing instruction.

«This isn't right, try again.»

«Too formal, and the example is from retail — my reader runs a café. Rewrite with a café example and shorter sentences.»

The first sends the model looking randomly. The second turns your reaction into a specification, which is the whole job.

blocks.text: Two rounds of correction beat any perfect prompt copied from the internet.

blocks.heading: A Loop That Ends
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Round one — brief, read, name the three biggest problems
  • Round two — fix those three, nothing else
  • Round three — polish by hand, because the last ten per cent is faster to do yourself

If you are on round six, the brief was wrong rather than the answer. Stop and rewrite the brief instead of nudging the same draft again.

blocks.question: You are on the fifth attempt and the draft is still not usable. What is the right move?

options.label: Keep going — one more attempt is usually the one that finally works.
Start again with a rewritten brief that includes what you have learnt.
Accept the closest version and spend the evening rewriting it yourself.
Switch to a different model and paste the same conversation into it.

blocks.successBody: Five failed attempts is not bad luck, it is evidence the brief is missing something. Restarting with what those attempts taught you is faster than pushing a conversation that has already drifted.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about what five similar failures are telling you about the instructions rather than the output.

blocks.heading: Where the Client Money Is
blocks.bodyHtml:
A client could run round one themselves. What they cannot do reliably is judge the draft — notice that the example is wrong for their audience, that the opening buries the point, that the tone will read as pushy.

You are being paid for that judgement. The tool produces text; you decide what is wrong with it. Nothing in this business is closer to the actual value you sell.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Take any draft you generated recently and list exactly three things wrong with it.
Write each as an instruction rather than a complaint.
Run one more round with only those three changes.
Note how long the whole loop took — that number is what you are selling.

blocks.heading: Keep the Corrections
blocks.bodyHtml:
The corrections you make repeatedly are your standing brief in disguise. If you have written «shorter sentences» three times, it belongs at the top of every prompt from now on.

Within a month this turns into a document that makes round one usable — and that document is genuinely worth more than any prompt collection you could buy.

blocks.body: Nobody gets finished work from a first prompt. Read the draft as a diagnosis, turn each reaction into an instruction, and keep the loop to two rounds plus a manual polish. When five attempts fail, rewrite the brief. The judgement in that loop is what a client is paying for.

modules.title: Writing People Pay For
modules.description: Sell writing that keeps a client's voice instead of sounding like everyone else. Covers briefs, structure, editing AI drafts, and what buyers check first.

lessons.title: What Makes Writing Worth Paying For

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Now that anyone can generate clean, grammatical text in seconds, it is reasonable to ask what is left to sell. If the writing itself is free, why would a business pay for it?

Because clean text was never what they were buying. They were buying someone who knows what the text is supposed to do — and that is the part the tool cannot decide.

blocks.heading: The Job Behind the Words
blocks.bodyHtml:
Every piece of paid writing has a job, and knowing it changes every sentence.

«Write a product description for a ceramic mug.»

«This mug is returned often because people expect it to be bigger. The description has to set the size expectation without making it sound small.»

The second is not a better prompt. It is a decision about what the writing must achieve, and nobody but you was going to make it.

blocks.text: Anyone can produce sentences now. Almost nobody knows what the sentences are for.

blocks.heading: Four Questions Before Writing
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Who is reading, and what do they already believe?
  • What one action should follow? Buy, reply, keep reading.
  • What objection is in their way? Price, trust, effort.
  • What must not be said? Claims they cannot legally or honestly make.

Answer these and even a mediocre draft lands. Skip them and a beautiful draft achieves nothing in particular.

blocks.question: A client says their landing page «isn't converting». What do you establish first?

options.label: Which tone of voice they would prefer the new version to be written in.
What visitors expect before arriving, and what stops them from buying.
How long the page should be and how many sections it needs overall.
Which competitors they admire, so the new page can match that style.

blocks.successBody: A page fails because of a mismatch between what the reader expected and what they found, or because an objection went unanswered. Tone, length and style are decisions you make after that, not instead of it.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which answer explains why people are leaving rather than how the page looks.

blocks.heading: Specifics Are the Product
blocks.bodyHtml:
Generated text drifts toward the general, because the general is the safest average of everything it has seen.

Your job is to put specifics back: the real objection, the real number, the real detail only this business knows. «Ships in 48 hours from Leeds» does more work than any amount of polished description, and no tool could have invented it.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Take any page from a business you like and answer the four questions for it.
Rewrite one paragraph using only those answers, without generating anything.
Now generate a version and compare which one contains real specifics.
Note which specifics you had to supply yourself — that is your paid work.

blocks.heading: Edit Like an Owner
blocks.bodyHtml:
The last pass is where the fee is earned. Cut every sentence that could appear on a competitor's site, replace adjectives with facts, and read it aloud to catch the phrases no human says.

Clients rarely have words for this, but they feel it immediately. «It finally sounds like us» is the whole review, and it comes from that pass rather than from the draft.

blocks.body: Businesses are not buying sentences, they are buying decisions about what the sentences must do. Establish the reader, the action, the objection and the limits before writing, then put real specifics back in and cut anything a competitor could have written.
blocks.nextTeaser: Next: capturing a client's voice so the work sounds like them, not like everyone.

lessons.title: Capturing a Client's Voice

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
«It doesn't sound like us» is the most common piece of feedback in paid writing, and the hardest to act on, because clients cannot usually explain what «us» is.

Voice feels mysterious for that reason. It is not. It is a small set of observable habits, and once you write them down it becomes something you can reproduce on purpose.

blocks.heading: Voice Is Six Observable Things
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Sentence length — short and clipped, or long and flowing
  • Person — «we» or «I», «you» or «customers»
  • Formality — contractions or none; slang or none
  • Humour — present, dry, absent
  • Vocabulary they own — the words they always use
  • Words they avoid — often more distinctive than the ones they use

Twenty minutes with three of their published pieces gives you all six.

blocks.text: Voice is not a mood. It is a list of habits you can write down and copy.

blocks.heading: Show, Do Not Describe
blocks.bodyHtml:
Adjectives are useless for transferring voice, because they mean different things to everyone.

«Write in a friendly, professional, approachable tone.»

«Match this: [paste two of their paragraphs]. Note they never use exclamation marks and always say «our team», never «we».»

Examples plus explicit rules will beat any tone description you can write, every time.

blocks.question: A client rejects three drafts saying each is «too corporate». What is the most useful next step?

options.label: Rewrite in a much more casual register with shorter, friendlier sentences.
Ask them to send two things they wrote that felt right, and copy the habits.
Ask them to define exactly what corporate means to them in their industry.
Suggest a call to discuss their brand values and positioning in more depth.

blocks.successBody: People recognise their voice far more reliably than they can describe it. Two examples they already approve of give you observable habits to copy, while asking for a definition returns another adjective.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which option gives you evidence rather than another word to interpret.

blocks.heading: Write the Voice Guide Once
blocks.bodyHtml:
Turn those six observations into a short document — half a page — and reuse it at the top of every request for that client.

This is also sellable on its own. Businesses pay for a voice guide, and you produce it as a by-product of work you were doing anyway. Few freelancers realise it is a product.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Pick a company and read three of their published pieces closely.
Note the six habits, with one real example of each.
Write a half-page guide, then generate something using it.
Compare against a version written without the guide.

blocks.heading: The Voice Is Not Yours
blocks.bodyHtml:
The most common quiet failure is a freelancer whose clients all sound the same — because they all sound like the freelancer.

Your preferences are not the standard. If you like short punchy sentences and the client writes long careful ones, the client wins. Clients notice this even when they cannot name it, and it is a large part of who gets rehired.

blocks.body: Voice is six observable habits: sentence length, person, formality, humour, owned vocabulary and avoided words. Gather them from real published work, show examples instead of describing tone, and write a reusable half-page guide — which is also a product clients will buy.
blocks.nextTeaser: Next: writing that survives being scanned rather than read.

lessons.title: Writing That Survives Being Scanned

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Most writing advice assumes a reader who starts at the top and continues to the bottom. Almost nobody does that on a screen.

People scan first and decide whether to read at all. So a piece can be well argued, accurate and clear, and still fail — because it was never given the four seconds it needed to earn the fifth.

blocks.heading: Front-Load Everything
blocks.bodyHtml:
Academic writing builds to a conclusion. Commercial writing puts it first.

«In today's competitive market, businesses face many challenges when it comes to…»

«Your product pages don't mention delivery times. That's the question filling your inbox.»

The first sentence is a warm-up nobody stays for. The second is the point, delivered before the reader decides to leave.

blocks.text: On a screen, the second paragraph is a privilege the first one has to earn.

blocks.heading: What Scanning Eyes Land On
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Headings — write them as statements, not labels: «Delivery is the question» beats «Delivery»
  • The first line of each paragraph — put the point there
  • Bold phrases — three or four per page, never a paragraph
  • Lists — anything with three or more items
  • Numbers — digits stop the eye where words do not

Written well, those five carry the whole argument to someone who never reads a full sentence.

blocks.question: Which heading works hardest for a reader who is scanning the page?

options.label: Delivery information and shipping options for your recent order
Most orders arrive in two days, and all of them are tracked
An overview of our approach to logistics and fulfilment
Frequently asked questions about delivery and returns policy

blocks.successBody: A heading that states a fact delivers information to someone who reads nothing else. Labels only tell the reader where they are, which is useful for navigation and useless for persuasion.
blocks.wrongHint: Ask which heading still says something useful if the reader never opens the section.

blocks.heading: Cut After Generating
blocks.bodyHtml:
Generated drafts are consistently too long, because more text always looks like more effort.

A reliable pass: delete the first paragraph, delete every sentence containing «in today's», and cut the length by a third. The piece almost always improves, which tells you what those words were doing.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Take a draft and read only the headings and bold phrases in order.
Ask whether that alone conveys the argument — if not, rewrite the headings.
Delete the opening paragraph and see whether anything is actually lost.
Cut the total length by a third and compare the two versions.

blocks.heading: One Idea per Paragraph
blocks.bodyHtml:
Long paragraphs are not hard because of the words. They are hard because two ideas were pushed together and the reader has to separate them.

Three sentences, one idea, then a break. This single habit does more for readability than any amount of vocabulary work — and it is the easiest thing to check before you deliver.

blocks.body: Readers scan before they read, so put the point first and make headings state facts rather than label sections. Carry the argument in headings, opening lines, bold phrases, lists and numbers. Cut generated drafts by a third, and keep one idea per paragraph.
