lessons.title: Why Good Clients Disappear After One Job

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
A job goes well. The client is pleased, says thank you, pays on time — and you never hear from them again. It is easy to read that as a quiet failure.

Usually it is not. They liked the work and then went back to their own problems, because nobody told them what the next step was. Repeat work is rarely won by being better; it is won by being suggested.

blocks.heading: The Sentence Almost Nobody Sends
blocks.bodyHtml:
At delivery, one line changes the shape of the relationship.

«Thanks, it's been great working with you — let me know if you need anything else.»

«The next obvious piece is the category pages — same format, same rate. Want me to pencil it in for the 20th?»

The first hands them a task: work out what they need and remember you. The second hands them a decision, which is much easier to make.

blocks.text: Clients do not leave because the work was poor. They leave because nobody named the next step.

blocks.heading: Three Natural Openings
blocks.bodyHtml:
• At delivery — highest goodwill, lowest effort, name one next piece
  • Two weeks later — ask how it performed; you get feedback and a reason to talk
  • At an obvious moment — a new season, a launch, a quarter starting

None of these is a sales message. Each is a specific, timely observation, which is why they work when a general check-in does not.

blocks.question: You delivered a job three weeks ago and heard nothing since. What is the best re-contact?

options.label: A friendly message saying hello and asking whether they need anything else.
Ask how the descriptions performed, and name the next set worth doing.
A discount offer on their next order to give them a reason to return.
Nothing — if they needed more work they would have contacted you first.

blocks.successBody: Asking about results shows you care what the work did rather than that it shipped, and naming the next set turns a check-in into a decision. A general hello puts the thinking back on the busiest person.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which message gives the client something concrete to say yes or no to.

blocks.heading: Ask What Happened Next
blocks.bodyHtml:
Very few freelancers ask about results, which is why the ones who do are remembered.

«Did the new descriptions change anything on the slower products?» costs one sentence. If the answer is good, you have a case study. If it is bad, you have a reason to be involved again — and either way you are the person still thinking about their business.

blocks.heading: Try
items: For each finished job, write the one obvious next piece of work.
Add that line to your standard delivery message.
Set a reminder two weeks after each delivery to ask about results.
List every past client you never followed up with, and message one today.

blocks.heading: Keep a Short List
blocks.bodyHtml:
Ten past clients you contact twice a year is worth more than a hundred strangers you contact once. They know you, they have paid you before, and the trust conversation is already finished.

Keep the list somewhere visible with the date you last spoke. That single column is the difference between a network and a folder of old emails.

blocks.body: One-off clients are usually clients nobody gave a next step. Name a specific next piece at delivery, ask about results two weeks later, and return at natural moments. Keep a short list of past clients with the date you last spoke — they convert far more easily than strangers.
blocks.nextTeaser: Next: turning that into monthly work instead of a series of one-offs.

lessons.title: From One-Off Jobs to Monthly Work

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Project work has a hidden cost that does not show up in the fee: every job needs finding, quoting, briefing and closing before it earns anything.

Monthly work removes most of that. The same money arrives with a fraction of the surrounding effort — and the client gets someone who already knows their business.

blocks.heading: Offer the Rhythm They Already Have
blocks.bodyHtml:
A retainer only makes sense when the underlying need repeats. Look at what they will need again anyway.

«Would you like to put me on a monthly retainer?»

«You add products most months — twelve descriptions a month at £150 instead of £180, and you stop having to ask.»

The first asks for a commitment. The second describes their existing routine with the friction removed, and prices it slightly better.

blocks.text: A retainer is not a bigger job. It is the same job with the asking removed.

blocks.heading: What Makes It Safe for Both
blocks.bodyHtml:
• A fixed quantity — «up to twelve» rather than «ongoing support»
  • A named month, invoiced on the same date each time
  • An exit — either side can stop with a month's notice
  • A rollover rule — unused work does not accumulate forever

Vague retainers are how freelancers end up permanently on call for a fixed fee. The quantity is what prevents that.

blocks.question: Which monthly offer is safest to take on, for both you and the client?

options.label: Ongoing content support whenever needed, billed at a flat monthly rate.
Up to twelve descriptions a month, invoiced on the first, monthly notice.
Priority access to your time at a reduced hourly rate for regular work.
A discounted bundle of hours to be used at any point during the year.

blocks.successBody: A capped quantity, a fixed invoice date and a simple exit make the arrangement predictable on both sides. Everything else here leaves the amount of work undefined, which always ends up defined in the client's favour.
blocks.wrongHint: Look for the option where both people know exactly what a month contains.

blocks.heading: Ask After the Third Job
blocks.bodyHtml:
The natural moment is the third repeat purchase. By then the pattern is obvious to both of you, and the offer sounds like an observation rather than a pitch.

«This is the third batch — shall we make it monthly and save you asking?» is almost always accepted, because you are removing a task from their list rather than adding a commitment.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Look at your finished jobs and find the one a client would need repeatedly.
Write it as a monthly offer with a capped quantity and a fixed date.
Add the notice period and the rollover rule in one line each.
Identify the client closest to a third repeat purchase and prepare the sentence.

blocks.heading: Do Not Fill Every Slot
blocks.bodyHtml:
Retainers are stable, which makes it tempting to take as many as you can. Fill your whole month and you have effectively taken a job — with no colleagues and no notice period.

Leave part of your capacity open for project work. That is where new clients, better rates and the freedom you started this for actually come from.

blocks.body: Retainers work when the underlying need already repeats: cap the quantity, fix the invoice date, agree notice and a rollover rule. Offer it around the third repeat purchase as an observation rather than a pitch — and leave part of your month open for new work.

lessons.title: Asking for the Referral

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Referrals are the cheapest clients you will ever get: no application, no competition, and the trust conversation is already over before you speak.

Most freelancers get almost none of them, and the reason is simple. They never ask, because asking feels like begging for favours from someone who already paid them.

blocks.heading: Make It Easy to Say Yes
blocks.bodyHtml:
A vague request puts the work on the client, who will not do it.

«If you know anyone who needs this kind of work, send them my way!»

«Do you know one other shop owner who adds products regularly? Happy for you to forward this — I've written the message so you don't have to.»

Asking for one person, with the text already written, is a request that takes ten seconds to grant.

blocks.text: «Anyone you know» asks for a search. «One person» asks for a name.

blocks.heading: Three Moments Worth Using
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Right after praise. When they say they are pleased, that is the moment.
  • At the end of a retainer month that went smoothly.
  • When you deliver results they can see and would happily repeat.

Outside those, a referral request feels like it came from nowhere. Inside them it feels like a natural continuation of the conversation you were already having.

blocks.question: A client emails to say they are delighted with the work. What is the strongest reply?

options.label: Thank them warmly and mention that you have capacity for more work.
Thank them, ask to use it as a testimonial, and ask for one introduction.
Thank them and send a list of the other services you can provide them.
Thank them and offer a referral discount for anyone they send to you.

blocks.successBody: Praise is the one moment when both a testimonial and an introduction are easy to give. Asking for one specific introduction rather than general awareness is what turns goodwill into an actual name.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which reply converts a good feeling into two concrete things you can use.

blocks.heading: Collect the Testimonial Then
blocks.bodyHtml:
Ask while they are pleased, and make it painless: «Could I use what you just wrote as a testimonial?» Almost nobody refuses their own words.

Waiting a month turns an easy yes into a request to compose something about work they have stopped thinking about — and that is why most freelancers have none.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Write your referral ask: one person, forwarding text included.
Write your testimonial ask as a single sentence.
Add both to your delivery routine so they are never improvised.
Send one of them today to a client who recently said something kind.

blocks.heading: Thank the Person Who Referred
blocks.bodyHtml:
When an introduction turns into work, tell the person who made it and thank them specifically.

It costs a message and is the single strongest way to get a second referral from the same person. Silence, on the other hand, quietly teaches them that the introduction went nowhere.

blocks.body: Referrals are the cheapest clients and the least asked for. Ask at the three moments when goodwill is highest, request one specific introduction with the forwarding text already written, and collect the testimonial in the same breath. Then thank whoever referred you, specifically.
